walkthroughs.body_html: Stars form in cold molecular clouds. Gravity collapses denser regions; falling gas heats up and forms a protostar. When the core reaches about 10 million K, hydrogen fusion begins.
On the main sequence, gravity pulling inward is exactly balanced by gas and radiation pressure pushing outward. This hydrostatic equilibrium keeps stars stable for millions to billions of years.
Low-mass stars use the proton-proton chain; higher-mass stars use the CNO cycle. Both net 4 hydrogen nuclei into 1 helium, releasing energy via mass-energy equivalence E = mc^2.
